setup: A pool of 100 loans is followed with no replacement of defaulted loans. Each year, 5% of the loans still performing at the start of that year default. Year 1 therefore produces 5.0 expected defaults.
ask: Expected defaults in year 5, compared with year 1:

options.label: Exactly 5
options.why: Applied the 5% to the original 100 loans every year. Defaulted loans leave the pool, so the base shrinks.

options.label: More than 5
options.why: Assumed default pressure builds with age. The rate is constant at 5% and the pool only gets smaller, so the count falls.

working.label: Loans alive at start of year 5

takeaway: A constant conditional rate applied to a shrinking pool gives a falling count of defaults.

setup: Moody's average cumulative default rates for Caa-C bonds: 27.867% by the end of year 2 and 36.908% by the end of year 3.
ask: The probability, seen today, that a Caa-C bond defaults during year 3 itself is:

options.label: About 28%
options.why: Read the year-2 cumulative figure, 27.867%. That is the wrong column and it still counts defaults in years 1 and 2.

options.label: About 37%
options.why: Read the year-3 cumulative figure, 36.908%. It counts every default in years 1 to 3, not only those in year 3.

takeaway: A year's own default probability is the difference of two cumulative figures, never one of them alone.

setup: Moody's cumulative default rates for Caa-C bonds: 36.908% by the end of year 3 and 44.128% by the end of year 4. The unconditional probability of default in year 4 is therefore $44.128\% - 36.908\% = 7.22\%$.
ask: The probability of default in year 4, given that the bond has survived to the end of year 3, is:

options.label: Equal to 7.22%
options.why: Left out the conditioning. The 7.22% is measured against all bonds alive today, including those that already defaulted.

options.label: Below 7.22%
options.why: Multiplied by the survival probability (63.09%) instead of dividing. Conditioning on survival raises the figure because the base is smaller.

takeaway: Conditional PD = unconditional PD divided by survival to the start of the year, so it is always the larger of the two.

setup: One-year rating migration, D is absorbing. A B-rated bond moves to A, B, C or D with probabilities 5%, 76%, 10% and 9%. Next year's default probability is 2% from A, 9% from B and 16% from C. The bond survives year 1.
ask: Which year-1 landing spot contributes the most to the probability of defaulting in year 2?

options.label: It moves to B, then defaults
It moves to C, then defaults
options.why: Picked the state with the highest default rate (16%) without weighting by the 10% chance of getting there: $0.10 \times 0.16 = 1.60\%$.

options.label: It moves to A, then defaults
options.why: Reversed the ranking. The safest rating is the least likely route to a default: $0.05 \times 0.02 = 0.10\%$.

takeaway: Weight each year-2 default rate by the chance of reaching that rating; the big, likely state beats the riskiest one.

setup: A firm has a constant hazard rate of 0.09 per year, in continuous time. It survives its first year.
ask: Compared with the probability of default in year 1 (as seen today), its probability of default in year 2, given survival, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Assumed survivors are safer. A constant hazard is memoryless: surviving a year changes nothing about the next year.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Assumed risk accumulates with age. That needs a rising hazard rate, and this one is constant.

takeaway: Constant hazard means constant conditional PD. The unconditional year-2 figure is smaller (7.87%) only because it is also weighted by survival.

setup: A company has a constant hazard rate of 2.1% per year, estimated from the CDS market.
ask: The probability, seen today, that it defaults during year 5 is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip, ten times too small. With survival still near 92%, year 5 defaults are about $2.1\% \times 0.92$, not a tenth of that.
Gave the cumulative probability to the end of year 5, $1 - e^{-0.105}$, which includes defaults in years 1 to 4.
Gave the probability of surviving to the end of year 4, $e^{-0.084}$, not a default probability at all.

takeaway: Year-5 default is roughly the hazard times survival to year 4, so a bit under the hazard rate itself.

setup: A counterparty's 3-year CDS spread is 375 bp with an assumed recovery of 75%. (Its 1-year CDS is 150 bp with 90% recovery.) Use the credit triangle: average hazard rate $\approx$ spread $/ (1 - R)$ over the 3 years.
ask: The average hazard rate over the 3 years is closest to:

options.label: About 3.75% per year
options.why: Used the spread itself as the hazard rate, leaving out the division by loss given default $(1 - R)$.

options.label: About 37.5% per year
options.why: Mixed maturities: divided the 3-year spread by the 1-year loss given default (10%).

takeaway: Use the spread and the recovery from the same maturity. A low recovery rate means each default costs more, so fewer defaults are needed to justify the spread.

setup: US municipal defaults arrive as a Poisson process at a constant average of 6.0 per year. The wait for the next default is exponential.
ask: The probability that the next default arrives within one month is:

options.label: Exactly 50%
options.why: Took the expected number of defaults in a month ($6/12 = 0.5$) as if it were a probability. The two agree only for very small values.

options.label: Above 50%
options.why: Reported $e^{-0.5} = 60.65\%$, which is the probability of NO default in the month, not of at least one.

takeaway: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$ never exceeds $\lambda t$, because the chance of two or more is counted only once.

setup: A bond trades at a spread of 250 bp with a 75% recovery rate. Under a stress scenario the spread widens to 480 bp and the recovery rate falls to 40%. Use a constant hazard rate with $\lambda \approx s/(1-R)$.
ask: Moving from the base case to the stress case, the 3-year survival probability:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Looked only at the wider spread. Dividing the stressed spread by the original loss given default gives $0.048/0.25 = 19.2\%$, but the loss given default has also risen to 60%.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: Assumed the two changes cancel exactly. The hazard rates are 10% and 8%, not equal.

takeaway: A wider spread does not always mean more default risk: if recovery falls faster, the implied hazard rate drops.

setup: A 2-year corporate bond yields 7% against a 3% risk-free rate, with 40% recovery. The credit triangle gives a constant hazard rate $\lambda = 0.04/0.60 = 6.67\%$ per year.
ask: The unconditional probability (seen today) of default during year 2 is:

options.label: About 6.67%
options.why: Treated the hazard rate as the year-2 default probability. Only the 93.5% of bonds still alive can default in year 2.

options.label: Above 6.67%
options.why: Gave the 2-year cumulative probability, $1 - e^{-0.1333} = 12.5\%$, which includes year 1.

takeaway: Marginal PD in a later year equals the hazard rate times survival to the start of that year, so it is smaller than the hazard.

setup: A one-year B-rated corporate bond has a credit spread of 2.2% over the maturity-matched T-bill. The recovery rate in default is 75%.
ask: The implied hazard rate (default intensity) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.55% per year
options.why: Multiplied the spread by loss given default $(1-R)$ instead of dividing by it.

options.label: ≈ 2.2% per year
options.why: Used the spread as the hazard rate, forgetting the division by loss given default.

options.label: ≈ 88% per year
options.why: Scale slip: $0.088$ read as 88%. A 2.2% spread cannot imply almost certain default each year.

takeaway: Spread over loss given default: with 75% recovery, the hazard rate is four times the spread.

setup: A company's 3-year and 5-year CDS spreads are 90 bp and 120 bp, with a 40% expected recovery. The average hazard rate is spread $/ (1-R)$: 1.50% over the first 3 years and 2.00% over the first 5 years.
ask: The average hazard rate between year 3 and year 5 is:

options.label: Between 1.50% and 2.00%
options.why: Averaged the two figures (1.75%). The 5-year average already contains three years at 1.50%, so the last two must be higher than 2.00%.

options.label: Exactly 2.00%
options.why: Reused the 5-year average as the forward rate. It is only the average of the first three and last two years together.

takeaway: Forward hazard = difference of cumulative hazards over the interval. When the average rises with maturity, the forward is above the longer average.

setup: Merton model. A firm's only liability is a one-year zero-coupon bond with face value 206.74m. A one-year European put on the firm's assets, struck at 206.74m, trades at 19.37m. The risk-free discount factor is 0.86, so the face value is worth $0.86 \times 206.74 = 177.80$m if it were risk-free.
ask: The market value of the firm's debt is:

options.label: Equal to 177.80m
options.why: Ignored default risk and priced the debt as if it were risk-free.

options.label: Above 177.80m
options.why: Added the put (177.80 + 19.37 = 197.17m). Bondholders are short the put, so it is subtracted.

takeaway: Risky debt = risk-free debt minus a put on the firm's assets: the creditors have written that put to the equity holders.

setup: Merton model. A firm is worth 200m and has one zero-coupon bond outstanding, face value 180m, due in 3 years. The risk-free rate is 5% (continuous) and asset volatility is 10%. Equity is a European call on the firm's assets with strike 180m.
ask: The value of equity today compared with 20m (the firm's value minus the face value of debt):

options.label: Equal to 20m
options.why: Used undiscounted intrinsic value $V - F$ and ignored that the 180m is only paid in 3 years.

options.label: Below 20m
options.why: Compounded the face value forward instead of discounting it ($180 e^{0.15} = 209 > 200$), which makes the option look out of the money.

takeaway: A call is worth at least $V - Fe^{-rT}$. Equity in Merton is more than $V - F$ because the debt is repaid later and the option has time value.

setup: A firm has a zero-coupon bond with principal 60m due at time T and no other creditors. At time T the firm's assets are worth only 50m.
ask: Equity at time T is worth:

options.label: Negative 10m
options.why: Subtracted the debt from the assets without limited liability. Equity holders cannot owe more than they invested.

options.label: Positive 10m
options.why: Took the size of the 10m shortfall as a gain. Here the creditors absorb the shortfall.

takeaway: Equity is a call on the firm's assets: $\max(V_T - D, 0)$. It can reach zero but never go negative.

setup: Merton model. A zero-coupon bond with face value 1,000 and 10 years to maturity is valued at 780. The continuously compounded risk-free rate is 1%.
ask: The bond's credit spread compared with 1%:

options.label: Equal to 1%
options.why: Assumed the bond is discounted at the risk-free rate alone. That would price it at about 905, not 780.

options.label: Smaller than 1%
options.why: Compared the yield with the 10-year risk-free accumulation (10%) instead of the 1% annual rate.

takeaway: Spread = $-\frac{1}{T}\ln(D/F) - r$. A 22% discount over 10 years is about 2.5% a year, far more than 1%.

setup: RedRose has a zero-coupon bond with face value 45m, now worth 40m, maturing in 3 years. Comparable risk-free bonds yield 2.5% (continuous).
ask: The bond's average credit spread is closest to:

options.why: Divided the spread by the 3 years a second time.
Stopped at the bond's yield and did not subtract the 2.5% risk-free rate.
Took $\ln(45/40)$ and forgot to divide by the 3 years.

takeaway: Yield per year first, then subtract the risk-free rate. The spread is a small difference of two annual rates.

setup: Merton model. A zero-coupon bond with face value 2m and 7 years to maturity is worth 1.2m today. The risk-free rate is 5% (continuous). The log discount is already done: $\ln(2/1.2) = 0.511$.
ask: The bond's continuously compounded yield is closest to:

options.label: About 51%
options.why: Used the log discount 0.511 as the yield and never divided by the 7 years.

options.label: About 5.0%
options.why: Set the yield equal to the risk-free rate. At 5% the bond would be worth $2e^{-0.35} = 1.41$m, not 1.2m.

takeaway: Divide the log discount by T to get an annual yield; only then compare with the risk-free rate.
